Abstract
Getting a precise estimate of electric fields around extra-high-voltage (EHV) trans-
mission lines is essential for keeping the public safe, ensuring environmental com-
pliance, and planning infrastructure effectively. Unfortunately, traditional numerical 
methods often struggle with accuracy and can be slow to converge, which makes 
them less suitable for large-scale projects. This study introduces a hybrid compu-
tational framework that combines the Charge Simulation Method (CSM) with the 
Firefly Algorithm (FA). This combination helps optimize the number, position, 
and strength of simulation charges, leading to better modeling accuracy and effi-
ciency. Additionally, we have trained three artificial intelligence (AI) models: 
Multilayer Perceptron Neural Network (MLPNN), Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Infer-
ence System (ANFIS), and Least Squares Support Vector Machine (LS-SVM) on 
real-world field data to reliably predict electric field values. Notably, LS-SVM is 
being used in this context for the first time and has shown to outperform the other 
models in accuracy, generalization, and speed. We evaluated the proposed CSM-FA 
hybrid model alongside AI predictions using metrics like Root Mean Square Error 
(RMSE), Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE), and the coefficient of determi-
nation (R2), revealing significant improvements over traditional methods. Given the 
heavy computational demands of the optimization and learning phases, we utilized 
high-performance computing (HPC) resources for implementation. This work not 
only advances algorithmic innovation and AI-assisted simulation but also enhances 
HPC applications, providing a scalable and precise solution for real-time field moni-
toring and regulatory assessments. The methodology aligns well with the scientific 
goals of The Journal of Supercomputing and fosters advanced research in intelligent 
power system modeling.

1  Introduction
The rapid global expansion of electrical energy demand, driven by unprecedented 
population growth and industrial development, has necessitated the widespread 
deployment of advanced high-voltage transmission systems operating at increas-
ingly elevated voltage levels. Modern overhead transmission lines, particularly those 
in the extra-high-voltage (EHV) range, now routinely employ bundled conductor 
configurations to enhance their performance and efficiency. While these technologi-
cal advancements facilitate more efficient power transmission, they simultaneously 
raise significant concerns regarding the environmental and health impacts associated 
with the electric and magnetic fields (EMFs) generated by these systems [1–4].
In response to these concerns, international regulatory bodies including the Inter-
national Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP)—endorsed 
by the World Health Organization—have established stringent guidelines limiting 
public exposure to EMFs [5–9]. These standards, which specify maximum permis-
sible levels of 5 kV/m for electric fields and 200 µT for magnetic fields, have been 
widely adopted as national safety regulations worldwide. Consequently, accurate 
modeling and prediction of electric field distributions around EHV transmission 
lines has become crucial for both regulatory compliance and public health protec-
tion [9].
From a computational perspective, modeling the electrostatic behavior of high-
voltage equipment is typically based in Maxwell’s equations. When the electric 
fields vary slowly over time, these equations simplify under the quasi-static approxi-
mation to Laplace’s equation, offering a computationally efficient framework for 
electrostatic analysis while maintaining engineering-level accuracy. However, in 
practical applications, transmission line geometries often involve irregular conduc-
tor shapes, multiple phase, and complex boundary conditions, which make analyti-
cal solutions to Laplace’s equation virtually intractable. Consequently, numerical 
approaches are essential for achieving reliable and accurate electric field evaluations 
[10–12]. Among these techniques, the Charge Simulation Method (CSM) that has 
emerged as a widely adopted method, due to its unique ability to accurate complex 
electromagnetic systems using a relatively sparse and manageable set of linear equa-
tions [13–15]. However, the precision of CSM is highly sensitive to the number, 
positioning, and magnitudes of the fictitious charges used, underscoring the need for 
an effective and automated optimization strategy [16, 17].
To overcome these limitations, this study proposes a hybrid optimization frame-
work that integrates the Charge Simulation Method (CSM) with the Firefly Algo-
rithm (FA) [17]. The CSM is efficient and straightforward, but its performance is 
highly sensitive to the choice and placement of simulation charges. By combining it 
with the FA a population-based meta-heuristic inspired by the flashing behavior of

In addition to physical modeling, our study integrates artificial intelligence (AI) 
techniques to predict electric field levels under varying operational conditions 
[18–21]. It can be employed three machine learning models Multilayer Perceptron 
Neural Network (MLPNN), Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS), and 
Least Squares Support Vector Machine (LS-SVM), All techniques were trained 
using field measurements obtained from a 400 kV transmission l line using a Mon-
roe Field Meter (Model 238A-1AC). MLPNN offers robust nonlinear approxima-
tion, ANFIS provides interpretability and adaptability while LS-SVM, used here for 
the first time in this application, it demonstrated a proven computational efficiency 
and improved accuracy through linear equation solving.
Among the artificial intelligence methods, MLPNN, ANFIS, and LS-SVM have 
been employed effectively to model complex and nonlinear systems in the engineer-
ing field [22–26]. The MLPNN is a highly nonlinear universal function approxima-
tor and can handle large high-dimensional data. It can capture complex input–output 
relationships effectively, yet it requires careful tuning of network parameters and 
may have slow training convergence. ANFIS originated from the fuzzy inference 
system and the learning capability of a neural network, and it provides a natural and 
simple framework that is effective when there is a degree of ambiguity or vague-
ness in the data. Its rule-based nature makes it interpretable but can restrict its scal-
ability and generalization, especially with large or noisy data. In contrast, LS-SVM 
can achieve good generalization performance at a relatively low computational cost 
by solving a set of linear equations, which is efficient for large-scale and real-time 
applications. Most importantly, these models are complementary in strengths, and 
their performance depends on the trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, and 
the speed of training and computation [27].
This study aims to advance both the precision and computational efficiency of 
electric field prediction models. Achieving these objectives is crucial in the realm of 
super-computing, where large datasets, rapid simulation cycles and scalable archi-
tectures are required. By combining hybrid optimization with AI-based learning, the 
proposed framework offers a dynamic and adaptable solution capable of handling 
complex field behavior across diverse transmission configurations. More than just 
a modeling improvement, this approach delivers practical advantages by reducing 
execution time, improving learning accuracy, and supporting iterative assessments 
required in grid design and regulatory studies. It also opens new pathways for real-
time field analysis, predictive safety systems, and the mitigation of induced effects 
in nearby infrastructure such as gas pipelines, rail systems, and communication 
networks.

2  Modeling and optimization of the electric field from overhead 
power line
Accurately estimating the electric field generated by extra-high voltage (EHV) over-
head power lines is essential for ensuring safety and compliance with electromag-
netic exposure limits. Due to the complexity of transmission line geometries and 
environmental conditions, numerical methods are often required. One of the most 
widely used techniques for such modeling is the Charge Simulation Method (CSM), 
which approximates the electric field by strategically placing fictitious charges 
around the conductor. While CSM is efficient and relatively easy to implement, its 
accuracy is highly sensitive to the number, location, and magnitude of these simu-
lated charges. To address this challenge, this study integrates CSM with the Fire-
fly Algorithm (FA), a meta-heuristic optimization method inspired by the natural 
behavior of fireflies. FA helps identify optimal charge configurations by exploring 
the solution space intelligently and avoiding local minima [14, 15].
2.1  Charge simulation method (CSM)
The charge simulation method (CSM) belongs to the family of boundary methods 
based on Maxwell’s equation, it has been frequently used to model the electric field 
distribution in high voltage euipment’s. In the charge simulation method (CSM); the 
modeling is based on the principle of substituting the surface density of actual elec-
trical charges of a conductor with discrete fictitious charges placed in appropriate 
positions inside around a fictitious circle. The magnitudes of these fictitious charges 
will be determined so that their integrated effect satisfies the boundary conditions of 
the potential applied to the conductor surface. Once the quantities of the fictitious 
charges are evaluated, the potential and electric field at any point outside the con-
ductor surface can be easily calculated according to superposition theorem using the

2.2  Firefly optimization algorithm (FA)
The Firefly Algorithm (FA) is a bio-inspired meta-heuristic approach, introduced 
by Xin-She Yang in 2008, it is a recent nature-inspired technique designed to solve 
nonlinear optimization problems. The algorithm is based on the principle of attrac-
tion between fireflies and simulates the behavior of a swarm of fireflies in nature. 
The algorithm takes the following three points into consideration [31–34]:
- All fireflies are unisex, what makes the attraction between them is not based on 
their sex.
- Attraction is proportional to their brightness, so for two fireflies, the less lumi-
nous will move toward the brighter. If no firefly is brighter than a particular firefly, 
the latter will move randomly.
- The brightness of the fireflies is determined based on an objective function (to 
be optimized). In the firefly algorithm, there are two important issues: variation of 
light intensity and formulation of attractiveness.

brightness is determined with objective function. So we cite four important points in 
the firefly algorithm: Light intensity, attractiveness, distance and movement. In the 
simplest form, the light intensity I(r) varies with distance r monotonically and expo-

3  Machine learning techniques presentation
The different types of machine learning approaches used in the prediction of the val-
ues for the electric field intensity caused under extra-high-voltage transmission line 
are based on the multilayer perceptron neural network (MLPNN), adaptive neuro-
fuzzy inference system (ANFIS) and least squares support vector machines (LS-
SVM) (Fig. 1).

4  Results and discussions
The optimized calculation and prediction of the electric field values at a height of 
1  m from the ground is limited to a single-circuit three-phase very high voltage 
400 kV overhead power line taken from the literature; whose data and geometric 
coordinates are shown in Fig. 5.
This electric field analysis involves two calculation steps. The first step consists 
of optimizing and evaluating the electric field generated by the studied power line 
configuration, using the charge simulation method (CSM) combined with the fire-
fly optimization algorithm (FA). The second step makes it possible to predict the 
electric field of the same configuration, by applying the multilayer perceptron neu-
ral network (MLPNN), adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS) and least 
squares support vector machines (LS-SVM).
4.1  The optimization and numerical calculation part
Before accurately calculating the electric field numerically by the CSM, it is neces-
sary to optimize the number and position of the simulating charges using the FA. 
The input parameters used in the firefly algorithm to solve the optimization problem 
are given as: Maximum number of generations G = 100; Population size Np = 20, 
Light absorption coefficient γ = 1; Attraction coefficient value β0 = 2; Mutation coef-
ficient α = 0.2.

4.2.1.2  Initialization of  parameters (ANFIS)  In the training phase of the Adaptive 
Neuro-Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS) for this study, a careful selection of param-
eters and functions was crucial for achieving accurate and reliable results. The mem-
bership functions for the input variables were defined using a triangular membership 
function (`typeMF = ’trimf’`), and a total of 11 membership functions were employed 
(`numMF = 11`). The output membership functions were set to have a constant type 
(`outmftype = ’constant’`), contributing to the interpretability of the system. The `gen-
fis1` function was employed with these configurations to initialize the fuzzy inference 
system using the provided training data. The resulting fuzzy inference system (`fis`) 
was specified as a Sugeno-type system with one input labeled ’input1’ and one output 
labeled ’output.’ The system comprised 11 rules, and the logical operations used in the 
rule base included ’prod’ for conjunction, ’max’ for disjunction, ’prod’ for implication, 
and ’sum’ for aggregation. The defuzzification method applied was the weighted average 
(`DefuzzMethod = wtaver`). During the training process, optimization parameters were 
fine-tuned, and display options were adjusted to provide comprehensive insights into the 
ANFIS training. This meticulous parameter selection aimed to enhance the robustness 
and efficiency of the ANFIS training procedure, contributing to the reliability of the 
subsequent inference and prediction tasks in the study.
4.2.1.3  Initialization of parameters (LS‑SVM)  In the process of implementing the Least 
Squares Support Vector Machine (LS-SVM), specific parameters and functions were 
utilized. The type of LS-SVM employed was tailored for function estimation. The tun-
ing of the LS-SVM involved determining the optimal values for the gamma (gam), 
sigma squared (sig2), and cost parameters. This optimization was performed using the 
’tunelssvm’ function with a grid search approach and cross-validation, where the goal 
was to minimize the mean squared error (mse) over seven cross-validation folds. Once 
the optimal parameters were determined, the LS-SVM model was trained using the 
’trainlssvm’ function with the Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel. The obtained model 
was then ready for further analysis and prediction tasks in the study (Table 1).

5  Conclusion
This study introduces a solid methodology for estimating and predicting electric 
field values around extra-high-voltage (EHV) overhead power transmission lines by 
blending numerical techniques with artificial intelligence (AI). The hybrid model, 
which combines the Charge Simulation Method (CSM) and the Firefly Algorithm 
(FA), effectively optimizes how we simulate electric field distributions. The FA 
boosts the accuracy of the CSM by figuring out the best number and placement of 
fictitious charges, resulting in efficient and reliable field modeling.
At the same time, three AI-driven predictive techniques: Multilayer Perceptron 
Neural Network (MLPNN), Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS), and 
Least Squares Support Vector Machine (LS-SVM) were trained on real-world meas-
urement data and assessed using metrics like RMSE, MAPE, R2, and computational 
time. Among these, LS-SVM stood out, outperforming both MLPNN and ANFIS 
by achieving the lowest RMSE and the highest regression accuracy, along with the 
quickest training time, making it the most suitable model for practical electric field 
predictions.
The results confirm the effectiveness of merging physics-based modeling (CSM-
FA) with data-driven AI predictions, providing a powerful tool for evaluating the 
impact of electromagnetic fields produced by high-voltage infrastructure. This inte-
grated framework not only enhances predictive accuracy but also aids in environ-
mental and safety assessments related to electromagnetic exposure. Additionally, 
this study marks the first time LS-SVM has been applied to electric field prediction, 
showcasing its potential for wider applications in electrical engineering challenges.
In conclusion, the hybrid approach and comparative evaluation presented here 
offer valuable insights for researchers and engineers looking for accurate, efficient, 
and scalable methods for assessing electric fields around transmission lines. Future 
research could delve into improved hybrid AI-optimization frameworks or apply

Abstract: Getting a precise estimate of electric fields around extra-high-voltage (EHV) trans- mission lines is essential for keeping the public safe, ensuring environmental com- pliance, and planning infrastructure effectively. Unfortunately, traditional numerical methods often struggle with accuracy and can be slow to converge, which makes them less suitable for large-scale projects. This study introduces a hybrid compu- tational framework that combines the Charge Simulation Method (CSM) with the Firefly Algorithm (FA). This combination helps optimize the number, position, and strength of simulation charges, leading to better modeling accuracy and effi- ciency. Additionally, we have trained three artificial intelligence (AI) models: Multilayer Perceptron Neural Network (MLPNN), Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Infer- ence System (ANFIS), and Least Squares Support Vector Machine (LS-SVM) on real-world field data to reliably predict electric field values. Notably, LS-SVM is being used in this context for the first time and has shown to outperform the other models in accuracy, generalization, and speed. We evaluated the proposed CSM-FA hybrid model alongside AI predictions using metrics like Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE), and the coefficient of determi- nation (R2), revealing significant improvements over traditional methods. Given the heavy computational demands of the optimization and learning phases, we utilized high-performance computing (HPC) resources for implementation. This work not only advances algorithmic innovation and AI-assisted simulation but also enhances HPC applications, providing a scalable and precise solution for real-time field moni- toring and regulatory assessments. The methodology aligns well with the scientific goals of The Journal of Supercomputing and fosters advanced research in intelligent power system modeling.
